mitigation_mechanism: Wetland storage lowers flood frequency and peak size and lengthens flood return periods.
caveats: Meta-analysis of existing wetlands (not restoration). Authors call the pooled flow-regulation effect medium; large site-to-site uncertainty that wetland traits do not explain.
justification: Kadykalo et al. (2016). The flow regulation services of wetlands. Ecosystem Services. — p.1: "We found that, consistent with conventional wisdom, on average wet- lands reduce the frequency and magnitude of ﬂoods and increase ﬂood return period; augment low ﬂows; and decrease runoff and streamﬂow." | p.4: "Fifty-nine weighted effect sizes were calculated from the 28 stu- dies, yielding a medium positive mean effect size"

mitigation_mechanism: Floodplain wetlands store floodwater; saturated upland (rain-fed) wetlands generate fast runoff.
caveats: Direction depends on wetland type and position: floodplain wetlands reduce floods, upland wetlands tend to generate them.
justification: Acreman et al. (2013). How Wetlands Affect Floods. Wetlands. — p.2: "Upland wetlands generally tend to be flood generating areas while floodplain wetlands have a greater potential to reduce floods." | p.3: "However, landscape location and configuration, soil characteristics, topography, soil moisture status and management all influence whether these wetlands provide flood reduction services."

mitigation_mechanism: Wetlands release stored water slowly, raising dry-season low flows.
caveats: Low-flow effect is not sized separately in the abstract (graded low by rule); the same review finds wetlands decrease total runoff.
justification: Kadykalo et al. (2016). The flow regulation services of wetlands. Ecosystem Services. — p.1: "We found that, consistent with conventional wisdom, on average wet- lands reduce the frequency and magnitude of ﬂoods and increase ﬂood return period; augment low ﬂows; and decrease runoff and streamﬂow."

mitigation_mechanism: A raised water table keeps peat wet, making fires less likely than on drained peat.
caveats: No size given (graded low by rule); fire risk on rewetted peat is not zero.
justification: IPCC (2014). 2013 Supplement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories: Wetlands. Chapter 3 Rewetted Organic Soils; Chapter 4 Coastal Wetlands / Inland Wetland Mineral Soils (chapter as applicable). IPCC, Switzerland. — p.119: "While the likelihood of fires on rewetted organic soils is considered low (particularly in comparison to drained organic soils), fire risk may still be real."

mitigation_mechanism: Rewetting drained peat attenuates fire risk.
caveats: Stated in passing in a section on restoration cost; no size (graded low by rule).
justification: Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (2025). Global Wetland Outlook 2025: Valuing, conserving, restoring and financing wetlands. Secretariat of the Convention on Wetlands, Gland. — p.55: "This illustrates the potential to increase the extent of peatlands under restoration with simple and cost-effective interventions (e.g., rewetting[125]) to reduce carbon emissions from drained organic soils, attenuate fire risk and enhance peatland biodiversity."
